items.body: In this edited extract of a conversation recorded at London's ICA on 25 March 2026 for the launch of Shock Factory: The Visual Culture Of Industrial Music, writer and art historian Nicolas Ballet talks to Cabaret Voltaire's Stephen Mallinder about sound, image and subversion Nicolas Ballet: In 1983, RE/Search Publications released the Industrial Culture Handbook, documenting the movement through a cultural project. This handbook, thanks to the introduction by music critic Jon Savage, clearly illustrated all the specific characteristics of the scene, and especially their shock tactics, conceived as a way to subvert the societies of control of that era. This publication included an interview with you and Richard Kirk, ten years after you founded Cabaret Voltaire in Sheffield with Richard and Chris Watson. We can also consult numerous references you provided at the end of the interview: recommendations of records, books, and films. Could you tell us about the context in which Cabaret Voltaire was created? How V Vale and Andrea Juno approached you to participate in this work, which will remain iconic in the field of industrial music? Stephen Mallinder: I should probably answer the second question first, because explaining how we started could easily become a lecture in itself. We began experimenting in 1973, but we didn’t think of ourselves as a band at that point. It wasn’t even just the three of us – there were probably half a dozen people involved. It felt more like a collective. And it wasn’t only about music: we were also interested in film, and everyone had different passions – some were into martial arts, others into cars. We were just teenagers, really, between 16 and 18, growing up in an industrial northern city. We were part of that environment, but at the same time we wanted to transcend it. We were drawn to other worlds – those we saw on television, in films, and heard on records. Over time, things gradually distilled down to three of us – Richard, Chris and myself – focusing on music. But it all started with a loose group of about ten people. There were various comings and goings: for instance, a guy called Mick was in the band for a while, but had to leave when his mother asked for the organ back he’d been playing. We were quite rebellious, but we had a strong interest in art and music, and we felt somewhat separate from many of the kids we went to school with. Eventually, it naturally coalesced into the three of us. Early on, we were particularly inspired by Roxy Music and especially Brian Eno during his time with the band. What fascinated us was the idea that someone could stand on stage with a tape recorder and a synthesizer – what we later learned was a EMS VCS3 – and create these strange, otherworldly sounds. To us, it was just a mysterious machine full of pins and patch cables. All three of us were drawn to that, and I think, in a way, we all wanted to be Brian Eno. That was really the origin. We then spent about three years simply experimenting. To jump ahead a bit: you mentioned ten years, but we had already spent quite some time with V Vale before that. We met him around 1979 or 1980, when we travelled to San Francisco to play a series of shows. At the time, we were signed to Rough Trade, which had launched an American label on the West Coast rather than in New York, believing it would be easier to establish something there. After releasing two albums, we moved over to the West Coast. We arrived in North Beach and were told, “You’re staying in this house.” The door opened, and there was Vale. He was – and still is – one of the most unique and brilliant people I’ve ever met. It turned out to be an extraordinary situation. Not only were we living in his house, right in the middle of North Beach, but he also ran City Lights Bookstore. Through him, we suddenly had a direct connection to William S Burroughs and the entire Beat movement. We found ourselves immersed in this strange, esoteric, and incredibly stimulating cultural world. The reason we later worked with Vale is simple: we lived with him. We shared that space with him, Andrea Juno, and Mark Pauline. At the time, Vale was just beginning what would become his Research series, but he was already publishing an extraordinary newspaper – not really a fanzine, but a large-format broadsheet – called Search & Destroy, which he co-edited with Andrea. We stayed close after that. We would return and spend time with him over the years. In fact, much later, if you look at the cover of The Covenant, The Sword And The Arm Of The Lord (1985), it features the three of us alongside Vale and Andrea. What connected us was the way he bridged art, literature, music, and attitude – he was deeply connected, and through him we became part of that wider cultural network, including the Industrial Culture Handbook. Vale later came to Sheffield and stayed with us for a while. He was an extraordinary character – one of the most beautiful people you could meet. I remember taking him on the train from London up to Sheffield. As the train passed through Leicester, he looked out of the window and exclaimed, “Oh my God – Leicester!” He was completely fascinated. For him, northern industrial England was exotic. He loved the canals, the rough pubs – everything about it. And he’s still out there, still active, still doing remarkable things. That’s how our relationship with him began, and why it lasted. NB: Yes, he’s still selling his own books, in front of City Lights in San Francisco! SM: Exactly, and the funny thing is, when we first knew him around 1979-1980, nobody knew Vale’s age. And we still don’t know, but he’s still going, so I think he’s immortal. I hope he is. NB: I hope too! Talking about Vale, he was very into, and still is today, the theories of William S Burroughs, such as you were, in a way, with Cabaret Voltaire and the cut-up technique, but through noise. And this is very interesting because it was a time when you defied order and control through noise. In the foreword you wrote for Alexander Reed’s book, Assimilate: A Critical History Of Industrial Music (2013), you said: “Although most at the time were unaware of many of the readings into the inherent political and social power of noise, it was clearly a language of subversion. Noise defied order and control. It was a musical taboo. Sonic belligerence. It could destabilise. This was not entertainment, but it was fun.” Regarding the fun part, could you tell us more about the first gig by Cabaret Voltaire in 1975? Because I understood it was a bit intense, especially for you. SM: Yes, I got thrown off stage and ended up in hospital. It’s become a bit of a legendary story. What’s funny is that, when you look back on it, there’s a certain strange logic to how it all unfolded. The whole thing ended in a riot – unsurprisingly, in retrospect. What we didn’t realise at the time was that we were playing in front of a crowd of engineering students whose main interests were rugby and beer. They weren’t exactly predisposed to experimental electronic music. And yet, that was our very first proper gig. In truth, the situation was something of a misunderstanding from the outset. We had spent a long time working in a loft, experimenting, staging odd happenings, even playing music to people randomly in the street – what you might call a kind of sonic terrorism. Eventually, we thought we should try performing in a more formal setting and see what would happen. The opportunity came through Chris. Someone he knew had a friend involved in an environmental group – something called Science For The People, I think – and they were organising a benefit concert. They asked Chris if his band would play. He said yes. When they asked what kind of music we made, he more or less told them whatever they wanted to hear: disco, pop, soul – everything. So we arrived having been billed as something entirely different. Instead, we came on stage playing tape loops and generating this dense, abrasive noise. There was also a visual element: projected film loops – probably Standard 8, before we even moved on to Super 8 – and Richard wearing a jacket covered in Christmas lights, plugged directly into the mains, which meant he could barely move. He was literally tethered to the electricity supply. I can’t remember us performing anything resembling a conventional song. We were just producing noise – intentionally so. Our idea of performance was rooted in chaos. We wanted to provoke a reaction, to create disruption. That, for us, was the point. And we certainly got a reaction. The audience stormed the stage, attacked us, and a fight broke out. Some friends helped pull us out of it, but it quickly escalated into a small riot. In the end, I was thrown off stage and ended up in hospital. It makes for a good story, but beneath it lies something more fundamental about our approach. From the beginning, our aesthetic was about shock, disturbance, and confrontation. That was our understanding of art at the time. Even the name Cabaret Voltaire was chosen for its provocation. The reference to Cabaret Voltaire – the birthplace of dada – carried an idea of disruption and anti-conformity that resonated with us. That was exactly what we were trying to do. NB: Yes, regarding the dada influence, you said that it “offered a guidebook of how to go about deconstructing a world that did not adequately represent the one we actually inhabited”. You also crossed paths with the members of Throbbing Gristle, who also released some Cabaret Voltaire recordings from the 1970s on Industrial Records. You shared with them a rejection of the British government of the time and the social and political difficulties it created. This system no longer allowed for belief in the hippie utopias of the 1960s. This critical perspective can be found in the album Red Mecca (1981), in which you criticised British participation in the war in Afghanistan by revealing “the dark heart of Thatcher’s Britain”, according to Martin Lilleker. The fact that the group was named after the Cabaret Voltaire says a lot about your approach. Did this link to art history serve to re-enchant reality, through a new relationship with art, a new way of thinking? SM: At that point in time, we were really trying to find fluid ways of expressing what we were doing. At the same time, we were very aware that, as individuals, we are inherently complex – and inherently political. We never wanted to separate our work from that dimension. Not in terms of party politics, but in the sense of recognising the inequalities and tensions that structure the world, and finding ways to point to them. Sound was one of our primary tools for doing that, but it wasn’t the only one – we also worked with visuals. What mattered to us was exploring different forms of expression, and how they could intersect. Red Mecca came out of that approach. It’s really about the power of words – the effect produced by placing two terms side by side. At the time we were working on it, we had also started making videos, and this coincided, quite strikingly in hindsight, with the Iranian Revolution. That context fed directly into our work. We incorporated imagery of Islamic fundamentalism, not in a purely critical or dismissive way, but as material to be juxtaposed. For instance, we would place images of Ronald Reagan alongside those of religious extremists. The word ‘red’ carries a whole range of associations – socialism, blood, violence – while ‘Mecca’ evokes a specific place, but also a broader idea of the East and of spiritual centrality. What interested us was precisely the tension between those meanings. We wanted to bring them together, almost collide them, without prescribing a fixed interpretation. It wasn’t about promoting a particular ideology. Rather, we were trying to provoke questions – to confront people with the contradictions of the world they inhabit. In a way, our work was about presenting those contradictions as they are, and saying: this is what surrounds you, this is what you’re living through. That was the impulse behind Red Mecca, and more broadly, what we were trying to do at the time. NB: The most conflicting aspects of the post-industrial system lead you to explore the theme of mind control, which is found in particular in the album The Voice Of America (1980). The titles “The Set-Up”, “Control Addict”, “Silent Command”, “War Of Nerves” or even “Spread The Virus” signal the group’s interest in the sort of mental conditioning you saw emanating from the US in the 1970s and 1980s. In the book Tape Delay (1987) by Charles Neal, you said: “We live and breathe like an American culture in England. It’s just throwing it back in another context.” These titles are also a clear reference to the idea that 'the word is a virus’ by William S Burroughs and his The Electronic Revolution. How did you approach the theme of mind control in the world of Cabaret Voltaire? SM: Yes, that was the world we were living in. It was just before Margaret Thatcher came to power, though her rise was already underway. At the same time, there was a strong awareness of American influence – what we would have understood then as a form of imperialism. What strikes me now is how relevant many of the themes we were engaging with still are, and also how their meaning has shifted. Take, for instance, The Voice Of America. At the time, we were interested in it as an example of media operating as a tool of influence, even indoctrination. Yet today, in a different context, it can be perceived as a voice of liberty. That kind of reversal is quite telling. More broadly, we were very attuned to the mechanisms of media. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, not everyone was thinking in those terms – but within certain circles, including groups like Throbbing Gristle, there was a growing awareness of how information and entertainment were becoming increasingly intertwined, and how propaganda functioned within that overlap. These are ideas that have become much more widely understood today, particularly with the rise of social media. But at the time, we were already thinking about questions of control – social control, the shaping of perception, the structures of power. Our references often came from literature, from writers like Franz Kafka, whose work explores precisely those kinds of systems. In a sense, what we were doing was simply reflecting those concerns back into the world – making them visible, or at least more perceptible. Looking back, it feels as though many of those concerns have only intensified, which perhaps explains why the work still resonates today. NB: What is fascinating about historical industrial groups is seeing how these artists anticipated very early on issues surrounding the media that are still relevant today. And we can also find different military elements in the artworks of Cabaret Voltaire, which could be compared to Industrial News, edited by Throbbing Gristle. Do you feel like you were taking part in the information war of industrial music at that time? SM: I don’t think we ever saw ourselves as partisan. The risk, when you take that position, is that you end up reproducing the very problem you’re trying to criticise. It’s a difficult balance – a kind of tightrope. We tended to think of ourselves more as observers, almost like journalists: taking what was in front of us and reassembling it, collaging it in a way that might allow people to see it differently. That was really the intention. The goal was simply to make people think – not to make them think like us. Everyone is free to draw their own conclusions. It was never our role to tell people what to think. That’s a trap you can easily fall into: believing you hold the truth, that you can somehow ‘liberate’ others by imposing a particular viewpoint. We wanted to avoid that entirely. The moment you start doing that, you risk becoming a form of propaganda yourself – part of the very problem rather than an alternative to it. What interested us instead was creating a shift in perception – presenting things differently, so that people might question them for themselves. NB: It could be violent and grotesque too at the same time. SM: I think another important aspect was our engagement with taboo. At the time, we approached it quite naively – we were younger, and it was very much of that moment. We deliberately played with subjects like militarism or overt political imagery because we felt that confronting those taboos could disrupt perception. The idea was to produce a kind of shock – something that might jolt people into a different awareness. With hindsight, I think we’re more cautious about that approach, and rightly so. We now have a better understanding of how people can be affected by these things, and how easily certain strategies can turn against their original intention. Part of the issue is that what begins as provocation can quickly be absorbed and neutralised. You only have to look at punk rock: something that started as a radical, disruptive force was rapidly co-opted, becoming commercialised and widely consumed. Once that happens, the original charge is lost. The same risk applies to working with taboo. Elements that were once confrontational can become aestheticised, turned into consumable objects. And at that point, their critical force is largely diminished. So I think it’s important to remain attentive to that dynamic. At least for me, there’s now a greater awareness of how these processes operate, and a corresponding need for caution. NB: Video was also a very important medium in Cabaret Voltaire. For example, you and Richard can be seen posing with a Portapack Sonore on the cover of The Crackdown. Video was so important that you started Doublevision in 1982 to release video works by Cabaret Voltaire and other industrial/experimental artists. The release of Doublevision Presents: Cabaret Voltaire allowed you to add moving images to your sound compositions, with the help of filmmaker St. John Walker for some videos. How did you approach this medium, at a time when music videos are increasingly commercialised worldwide? SM: I think it comes from the fact that we never really saw ourselves as musicians so much as artists. That gave us the freedom to move between different media quite naturally. In fact, even before the concert we mentioned earlier – the one that ended in a riot – we had already staged what you might call our first performance. It took place at the Edinburgh Festival fringe, probably the summer before. The only problem was that we couldn’t afford the train fare to get there, so we didn’t attend in person. Instead, we created what we called a ‘concert package’. We sent it to the festival, and it was presented in our absence. It consisted of a reel-to-reel tape, a Super 8 film, and a series of printed handouts – cut-ups and montages. In other words, it contained all the elements of a performance, just without the performers. The audience experienced it as a kind of distributed concert. We later learned that Lol Coxhill was present and even played along with the material as it was being shown, which is quite extraordinary. But we weren’t there – the film was screened, the tape was played, and the audience engaged with the printed material. That approach says a lot about how we thought from the beginning. We were always interested in multimedia, in combining different forms. As technology evolved – particularly in electronic music and film – it became more accessible and easier to use, which allowed us to push that integration further. We started with Super 8, but as soon as new tools became available – video, then later digital cameras – we adopted them immediately. It wasn’t about being purist or attached to a specific format; we were interested in what each medium could offer. Super 8, for instance, could be transferred to video, which made it much more malleable as a material. Our influences were already pointing us in that direction. Beyond Roxy Music, we were deeply inspired by The Velvet Underground, as well as by Andy Warhol and his Exploding Plastic Inevitable (1966-1967). The idea that images could create a kind of hypnotic texture – just like music – was very important to us. So, visuals were always part of what we did. By the 1980s, the available technology simply made it easier to integrate them more fully into our work, and we embraced that without hesitation. We were never interested in limiting ourselves to one medium – we wanted to use everything that was available. NB: Your video practice aligned with the spirit of the industrial genre, both in its multidisciplinary nature and in the topics you addressed through this medium; in Doublevision Presents, you used footage of New Guinean tribes and Shiite rituals, but also images from pop culture and other various sources (medical procedures, military parades and riot footage), captured either from the television news or from the archives. How did you come up with the idea of ​​working with these different archives? SM: I’m not sure I can give a single, definitive explanation. As you were describing it, what struck me is how much of it relates to ritual. That’s something we’ve always been drawn to – those forms of behaviour through which people try to make sense of the world. We’ve consistently been interested in what you might call the esoteric, or practices that exist on the margins. For instance, much later, when we made “Don’t Argue” (1987) in America with Peter Care, we included documentation of an actual voodoo ceremony. That kind of material fascinated us – not in a purely anthropological sense, but as a way of engaging with systems of belief and representation. At the same time, there was a strong interest in working with found footage: bringing together contemporary images, television broadcasts, archival material, old films. That impulse was always there. But beyond that, it was really about process. Our method was based on montage and juxtaposition – placing things side by side and seeing what emerged from that encounter. Often, the results were unexpected. We would discover connections or tensions we hadn’t anticipated. In our live performances, for example, the visuals and the music were constantly shifting, and the way they aligned was never fixed. Each iteration produced a different set of relationships. What mattered to us was precisely that moment of collision. We weren’t aiming for coherence in a conventional sense. The work wasn’t meant to make sense in a linear or unified way. Instead, it was about creating points of friction – instances where images and sounds collide, fragment, and recombine into something new. In that respect, the material itself often came from places others might overlook or avoid. We were drawn to what lay at the margins – discarded images, overlooked footage, fragments found on the periphery. Those were the elements we wanted to bring into play. That, ultimately, is what guided our approach. NB: This may also be a way of showing the paradoxes of Western societies between violent images and more consensual images in popular cinema and popular culture in general. SM: Yes, absolutely. We still live in an intensely violent society, and there’s always a risk of turning away from that reality. What has changed, perhaps, is the way that violence is mediated. Today, we exist in what Guy Debord described as the ‘society of the spectacle’, where everything becomes image, performance, and representation. In that context, the distinction between what is real and what is constructed becomes increasingly difficult to grasp. When we were working, there was a stronger sense – at least from our perspective – that what we were engaging with remained more directly connected to lived reality. Now, I think many people struggle to locate a reality that feels stable or coherent. There’s a sense of living within a kind of simulation, where experience is constantly mediated and reframed. In a way, it feels as though we were anticipating some of these developments, even if we didn’t fully articulate them at the time. What we were doing was rooted in that specific moment, but looking back, it also seems to resonate strongly with the present – particularly in terms of how we understand media, perception, and reality itself. This is something I’ve been thinking about again recently, especially with the renewed activity around Cabaret Voltaire. It brings into focus the extent to which earlier work now reads almost as a form of prefiguration. At the time, though, much of it was intuitive. We didn’t necessarily have a fully formed theoretical framework for what we were doing – we were artists, and we were working instinctively. It’s really only in retrospect that some of those ideas begin to take on a clearer shape and meaning. NB: You also composed the soundtrack for Peter Care’s film Johnny YesNo (1982). I guess the working method was very different here: did you adapt to the film, or did Peter Care direct his shots according to your universe? SM: We didn’t really know how to approach it at the time – we had to invent our own method as we went along. No one was telling us how to compose a film score. We worked directly with the rushes that Peter Care brought into the studio. He would come down, we’d project the footage onto the wall, and we would simply play along to it. In that sense, it was almost like performing a live soundtrack. That’s how the ideas emerged: by responding in real time to the images. There wasn’t much room for editing or rearranging. We couldn’t manipulate the material in the way you can today. Instead, we focused on capturing the atmosphere of each scene – finding the right mood and playing to it as it unfolded. It was very immediate, very instinctive. I imagine the process is quite different now. Contemporary composers often construct soundtracks with a high degree of precision, using digital tools to map sound to image. At the time, though, it was much more direct – we were essentially making it up as we went along. But it worked for us, and it was a lot of fun. In many ways, scoring Johnny YesNo felt like playing a live concert. We approached it with the same energy and responsiveness. We also had an ongoing relationship with Peter Care, which made the collaboration very natural. Around the same period, we worked on other projects in a similar way. For instance, we contributed to Salvation! (1988), and New Order were also involved in film scoring at the time. The approach remained largely the same: we received the rushes and responded directly to them. There were no digital timelines, no screens to synchronise everything in advance. You created the soundtrack first and then found ways to align it with the images afterwards. It was a very hands-on process. The same applies to Chance Versus Causality (1979), made with Babette Mondini. That piece was recorded in the studio in a single live take. Nicolas Ballet would like to thank the ICA team, especially Hannah Geddes, Eray Yilmaz, Tom Heardman, Steven Cairns, Ken Eno and Beni Asante, as well as Stephen Mallinder's manager, Steve Malins. Shock Factory: The Visual Culture Of Industrial Music is published by Intellect. The Wire 499 featured a ten page special of essays and interviews exploring the visual and sonic world of Cabaret Voltaire. Buy a copy of the issue here. Subscribers can read the issue online in the digital archive.
items._cn_summary: 本文是The Wire杂志刊登的一段对话实录，记录了作家Nicolas Ballet与Cabaret Voltaire成员Stephen Mallinder在伦敦ICA的访谈。内容围绕工业音乐视觉文化展开，追溯了Cabaret Voltaire于1970年代在谢菲尔德的成立过程，最初由约十人的松散群体逐步凝聚为三人组合。乐队深受Roxy Music及Brian Eno影响，尤其是Eno在舞台上使用磁带录音机与EMS VCS3合成器创造的奇异声响，成为他们追求实验性声音美学的起点。文章涉及工业音乐运动的文化语境、RE/Search Publications的《Industrial Culture Handbook》等关键文献，以及乐队对反叛精神与跨领域艺术探索的态度。作为工业音乐与电子实验领域的先驱，Cabaret Voltaire的历史脉络对理解后朋克、电子与工业声响的交汇具有重要参考价值。

items.body: Review by andrea — "Sunlight" is the second album by Drift Lab, a jazz rock project based in Rome and led by Manuele Montesanti. It was self-released in 2026 with a completely renewed line-up featuring, along with founder member, composer and leader Manuele Montesanti (piano, synths), the new members Marco Pistone (bass), Guido Della Gatta (guitars) and Roberto Porta (drums) plus the guest Carlo Maria Micheli (sax). According to the official website, this is music "written with rigour but performed with freedom, where improvisation finds its home within intricate harmonic architectures". Drift Lab is an open, constantly evolving project, aiming to shape a sound that blends "jazz roots and contemporary imagery, instrumental virtuosity and electronic curiosity, composition and experimentation". The art cover tries to give a visual form to the musical content...Electronic sounds and a brief drum roll introduce the album's title track, "Sunlight". It's a bright piece, full of frenetic energy, ready to wake us up to face a new busy day. A kind of urban ride illuminated by the sunlight...The following "Yellow Fire" is a piece with a jagged rhythm but full of warmth and melodic flares that leads to "Bump" a jazz rock track full of nocturnal and disquieting atmospheres with excellent interweaving of guitar and keyboard that share the solo parts, supported by a never banal rhythm section..."A-M-M-I-M" somehow revisits and reinterprets a piece from the previous album ("M-I-M-M-A"). It's a relaxed track that at times invites you to dance the night away while "Serendip" is a slow, sensual piece featuring guest saxophonist Carlo Maria Micheli and a certain oriental exoticism. The title refers to the ancient name of the island of Ceylon..."Chaste Countrywoman" starts with the bass in the foreground that traces a funky rhythm, then the electric guitar outlines melodic paths that take the song in other directions... Next comes "Bleep" is a complex and fast piece where all the musicians showcase great technical skills and a notable interaction."bYpOLAR" begins with an old video-game atmosphere and continues with irrepressible freshness, alternating more relaxed moments with others where the pace becomes pressing and lively. Ten, the dreamy "Evolving" concludes the album. A beautiful official video was shot for this piece, completing the sonic universe the band has evoked with images of a disturbingly beautiful dystopian future...On the whole, an excellent fusion work!
items._cn_summary: 意大利罗马爵士摇滚融合项目Drift Lab的第二张专辑《Sunlight》，由钢琴家兼作曲家Manuele Montesanti领衔，融合爵士即兴、摇滚节奏与电子声响，并融入部分世界音乐元素（如"Serendip"中带有东方异域色彩，呼应斯里兰卡古称）。专辑强调"严谨的写作与自由的演奏"，在复杂的和声结构中留出即兴空间。曲目风格多样，从同名曲的城市律动感，到"Bump"的夜晚不安氛围，再到"A-M-M-I-M"的放松舞蹈性以及"bYpOLAR"的复古电子游戏氛围，层次丰富。独立发行，制作精良，兼顾技术性与可听性，对融合跨界与即兴演奏感兴趣的听众值得关注。

items.body: Montréal-based darkwave and dark synthwave producer Das Mörtal has released the double single “Parasite & Ghost” via Lisbon Lux Records. The release also serves as a preview of the forthcoming mini-album “DECVY I,” scheduled for October 29, 2026, on the same label. The double single pairs two tracks that occupy distinct stylistic territory. “Parasite” is described as a fast-paced darkwave track about illness. Regarding the track, Das Mörtal says: “An illness has affected my body for some time now, and Parasite was made under a pain that I can’t quite shake off.” “Ghost” is a witch-house-infused pop single, with catchy vocal melodies and driving kick drum-infused percussion. Alongside the double single, Das Mörtal has announced “DECVY I,” a mini-album due October 29, 2026, via Lisbon Lux Records. About Das Mörtal Das Mörtal is the project of Cristobal Cortes, a Santiago, Chile-born producer who grew up in Montréal. His musical journey began in Berlin, where he relocated roughly a decade and a half ago seeking electronic music with a more aggressive, punk-oriented edge than the minimalist house and techno sound that dominated the Montréal scene at the time. In Berlin, Cortes encountered the DJ culture of clubs associated with Ellen Allien’s BPitch Control label, an experience that informed his understanding of dancefloor dynamics and formed his subsequent production approach. Back in Montréal, Cortes developed the Das Mörtal project and found a label home in Lisbon Lux Records, a Montréal-based imprint that helped disseminate his music internationally. His debut album “Always Loved” was followed by further EPs and singles, and his catalogue expanded to include the full-length “Bury To Sorrow” (October 2023), a twelve-track record featuring a collaboration with Dance With the Dead. An instrumental version of the album was released in May 2024. His most recent work before the current release was the EP “Origins” (October 17, 2025), which included the single “Falsche Daten” ORIGINS EP by Das Mörtal And now there is the double single “Parasite & Ghost”. “DECVY I” follows on October 29, 2026, on the same label.
items._cn_summary: Das Mörtal 是来自蒙特利尔的暗潮与暗合成波制作人 Cristobal Cortes，新作双单曲《Parasite & Ghost》由蒙特利尔独立厂牌 Lisbon Lux Records 发行，作为迷你专辑《DECVY I》的前瞻。《Parasite》为快节奏暗潮，主题围绕疾病与身体痛苦，《Ghost》融合巫术浩室元素，兼具抓耳人声旋律与强劲打击乐底鼓。Cortes 拥有智利出生、蒙特利尔成长、柏林电子乐场景浸润的多元背景，其作品融合了 BPitch Control 时期以来的俱乐部动力学与暗黑电子美学。此文为厂牌新闻通稿性质，缺乏深入的艺术评论与声响分析，信息以发布信息与艺术家履历为主。整体音乐定位偏向暗潮/电子交叉地带，符合小众地下电子乐审美。

items.body: A fan (interesting that we are being informed this way in 2026) of the Portland EBM duo Puerta Negra informed us that they have released the lead single and official video for “Complejo de Victima,” the first track issued from their EP “Metafísica,” due June 12, 2026 on Oráculo Records. The single is sung entirely in Spanish, with vocals by María Aguirre, and its video was directed by Zach Flanary. Oráculo Records is a Spanish label whose recent catalogue Side-Line has covered through labelmate releases such as Neon Electronics’ “Liberation”. “Metafísica” will be the duo’s third release, following the 2022 debut “Costo Humano” and the 2023 EP “Playa Sola.” A vinyl edition will also be available for pre-order through the label’s Bandcamp page. Metafísica by Puerta Negra The EP runs to six tracks: “Ventana Cerrada,” “Quien Es tu Dios,” “Complejo de Víctima,” “Explosión Cósmica,” “Después Del Cuerpo,” and “Ojo De Aguja.” The video for “Complejo de Victima,” which translates as “victim complex,” was directed by Zach Flanary and shot in black and white. About Puerta Negra Puerta Negra is a duo from Portland, Oregon, formed by María Aguirre and Mark Arciaga. Aguirre, who handles vocals, previously played in Vueltas; Arciaga came from Lizard Skin. The project takes its name from the Los Tigres del Norte song “La Puerta Negra” and writes its lyrics in Spanish. The debut “Costo Humano” arrived on March 8, 2022 through the Berlin label Detriti Records, issued on cassette as a run of 40 copies. The six-track release was co-produced and mastered by Susan Subtract. Oráculo Records later pressed “Costo Humano” to vinyl, on 180-gram black vinyl mastered by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany. In 2023, the duo released the EP “Playa Sola” through the New York label Synthicide, a 12-inch pressing limited to 250 copies with a full-colour insert. KEXP featured the track “Caída al Mal” as a Song of the Day in May 2023. The duo’s discography is documented on Discogs; no Wikipedia entry for Puerta Negra was found. “Metafísica” continues the duo’s work with Oráculo Records, which previously handled the vinyl edition of “Costo Humano,” and is set for release on June 12, 2026.
items._cn_summary: 波特兰EBM二人组Puerta Negra即将在西班牙独立厂牌Oráculo Records发行EP《Metafísica》，延续其以西语演唱的电子工业路线。乐队由María Aguirre和Mark Arciaga组成，名字取自Los Tigres del Norte的歌曲，作品融合暗黑电子节奏与拉丁文化语境。此前两张作品分别由柏林Detriti Records和纽约Synthicide发行，限量卡带与黑胶制作体现了地下厂牌的美学坚持。整体定位为带有西语文化视角的独立EBM，风格偏向暗潮/工业电子范畴，但本次内容为新闻通稿性质，未涉及对实际音乐创新性或声响设计的深入评析。

items.album: Treble Puns Release A Concept Album Alternating Between Comical Skits & Sombre Post-Rock Jams

items.body:
Treble Puns, the Bangalore duo of Sohini Bhattacharya and Abhimanyu Roy, just released their new album 'Life Lessens 1: A God Named Frank'.

While their last release, 'Chill Ke Armaan', saw them take a break from their usual existential meanderings for irreverent humour, the latest record manages to do both over its 9 tracks of sombre jams, bookended by and alternating with comical skits that come underscored by sitcom-style music. They present a story of Frank, the junior God of honesty, who slept for millennia to wake up in the present times. At least, that is the device with which the band discusses things like the secret to happiness and satisfaction, vocally on 'Zen Commandments?' and then musically on 'Hey... Are You Happy?', or of the pressure to create content and market on social media instead of just being artists on the skit 'The Pursuit Of Crappiness', followed by 'Dog Eat Dog World'.

In times when through-listening of albums is on a decline in people's staple consumption habits to benefit concept albums, the skits on 'Life Lessens 1: A God Named Frank' slip into the ear more like a musical podcast (we are sure the characters on the skit will have something to say about this). The musical tracks, on the other hand, present some compositionally strong post-rock jams, limited mostly by the production value behind capturing the duo's energy on their respective instruments of drums and guitars that come supported with layers of synth.

Treble Puns even adds lyrical vocals to the fold for the first time. It works well when it joins the wall of sound that the band conjures, while the more unobscured verses on 'Hey... Are You Happy?' or 'Dog Eat Dog World' are clearly the limiters of the emotional profundity that the band creates with its guitar lines and drum replies. Away from such faultlines, 'Life Lessens 1: A God Named Frank' isn't just to be lauded as an interesting and ambitious album conceptually, but for being able to provide revisitable jams like 'Probably a Bad Idea' and the new directions signalled by the almost entirely electronically programmed 'Dog Eat Dog World'.

Listen to the album below and follow Treble Puns for more.

items.body: A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene's outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There's a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout. The opener, "Svennedal," with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer's impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to "Nordgård," the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus. Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional "Agnete Of Bjergmanden," with Guldhammer's soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, "Ormsø," mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental. Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning – what will GuldGanger do with an entire album? Find the artist online. Further reading and listening: Mats Edén - Tellef Kvifte - Knut Kvifte Nesheim - Króta (Review) Duo Ruut - Ilmateade (Review) Floating Sofa Quartet - Sofa Songs (Review) Search RootsWorld Subscribe and Support RootsWorld

items.body: Króta, the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Edén has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sjøfløyte, more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim, a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects.
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: Króta是挪威Taragot厂牌发行的跨斯堪的纳维亚民谣合作专辑，由瑞典小提琴家Mats Edén与挪威音乐家Tellef Kvifte及其子Knut Kvifte Nesheim组成。作品以瑞典和挪威传统曲调为基础，融合多种乐器配置，包括竖笛、萨克斯和风笛等非传统挪威民乐乐器。三位音乐人均有跨界探索经历，乐评中提到他们致力于模糊不同音乐流派之间的界限，使作品在传统民谣框架中融入爵士即兴与跨风格元素。整体定位介于北欧传统民谣与世界音乐融合之间，对熟悉斯堪的纳维亚民间音乐传统的听众具有参考价值。

items.body: It's been a lengthy wait for the fourth album from Finnish accordionist Teija Niku, but she's hardly been idle over the last few years. Between the pandemic, giving birth, and the death of her mother, her time has been filled. But the long pause makes this return all the sweeter, with its joyful exploration of the places where the music of her homeland intersect with her deep love of Balkan music. That's amply illustrated on her composition "Finsko Dajchovo," inspired by the Bulgarian folk dance rhythm, a loving creation that moves sprightly and gracefully, or "Seitsemän," taking its cue from Macedonian love songs. The bright, springlike melody, light, full of promise and hope could have been written for eager dancing feet. Everywhere, Niku displays her acute sense of melody. "Elokuu," a celebration of the late summer lights of August, is a lilting, wistful piece, yet tinged with shades of melancholy for the winter to come, a masterful evocation of shifting moods. While the influence of Balkan music hovers over Tovi (the title, according to Niku, translates as "an undefined bit of time, somewhere between a moment and a while"), a Nordic sensibility remains very much at its heart, with a couple of soaring polskas to move things briskly along, in a contrast to the brief, shadowy, brooding opener "Ohto." But the real heart of the disc comes at the very end, with "Poloneesi äidille," a piece Niku composed for her mother's 70th birthday, three years before she died. It's a soft, elegiac work that suddenly becomes transcendent as she begins to sing, You can hear that this performance is completely from the heart, and it is a beautiful way to finish. Now to hope that it's not such a long gap before she's back in the studio.
items._cn_summary: 芬兰手风琴演奏家Teija Niku的第四张专辑《Tovi》，将北欧民间音乐传统与巴尔干音乐元素相融合。专辑以保加利亚民间舞蹈节奏为灵感的原创曲目开篇，融入马其顿情歌元素，同时保留北欧音乐的内敛气质。手风琴演奏突出旋律感，作品在轻快波尔卡舞曲与沉思抒情段落之间交替展开。专辑结尾的《Poloneesi äidille》是为已故母亲七十岁生日创作的三年前作品，加入人声演唱，情感深沉真挚。整张专辑呈现北欧与东南欧音乐文化的跨界对话，定位为跨文化世界音乐融合作品，兼具地域特色与个人情感表达。

items.body: This collaboration between the five-piece Belgian instrumental group Wör, whose members specialize in bringing the music of earlier centuries to life, and Kongero, the acclaimed Swedish female acapella folk quartet, offers an unusual chance to explore how their two cultures, ostensibly so different, can come together. It might sounds an unlikely mix, but here's a spoiler: it turns out they're pretty much musical best friends. The album kicks off at a cracking pace with "Var Är Du?", a bravura performance through a twisted, tortuous piece that manages to be both elegant and surprising. However, the true astonishment arrives at the end, when the audience applauds and you suddenly realize this was recorded live (actually over two separate performances). The musicians bring material from their separate traditions, plus one original, showcasing their skills in intricate, swinging arrangements for both instruments and voices. Thanks to their skill, the varied ideas fit together seamlessly so it's brimming with delights, like the wonderfully-titled "Drinking Like A Sweet Swede," where the singers layers their harmonies over a jaunty backing. Everything is intricate, performed with a glowing precision that can disarm the senses with its beauty. The highlight, perhaps, is the beautiful "Klosterjungfrun." The slow, seductive opening draws in the listener, the voices airy and light, curling around each other as the instruments wind long their path their. It's a beautiful piece, but really, just one gem among so many here. There's never a foot wrong, no note out of place and the performances are passionate, stellar, a true collaboration of instruments and voices. Add to that a mix that's sharp as a razor, and Songbooks Live is a truly outstanding album, a perfect illustration that people have more in common than separates them. And it illustrates exactly what artists can achieve live. With luck, they'll work together again. Soon, please.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张比利时早期音乐器乐团体WÖR与瑞典无伴奏民歌女声四重唱Kongero的合作专辑，融合了欧洲早期器乐传统与斯堪的纳维亚民歌人声。专辑以现场录音呈现，编曲精密而灵动，器乐与人声交织自然，展现了两种文化之间的共性。曲目从复杂的器乐编配到空灵的人声和声均有涉猎，层次丰富，制作清晰锐利。整体定位介于世界音乐、欧洲早期音乐与跨界融合之间，强调传统技法的精妙与文化对话的可能性，但实验性与前卫性有限，更偏向精致的传统融合路线，对偏好世界音乐与跨界合作的听众有较强吸引力。

items.body: McDowell County West Virginia is nestled in the Appalachian Mountains, and is both stunning and isolated. But, since coal's heyday has long past, it is also considered the poorest part of the state, if not the entire country. With perhaps as much as 30% unemployment and low average annual incomes, it, like much of the coal regions that surround it, is horrifyingly depressed. It is also overwhelmingly white, and went hard for Trump, boasting the largest support for him in the country in 2016. In 2023, The Guardian ran a photo exhibit on what was designated to be West Virginia's "last snake handling church." The photos, taken at The House of Lord Jesus, in Squire, deep in McDowell County's claustrophobic, coal scarred southwest, depict stark black and white images of an elderly woman burning a kerosene flame near her face, lots of snakes, and people seemingly possessed as they surrender to a form of Pentecostal practice that uses a quote from Mark 16:18 as their raison d'être. "They shall take up serpents...," the verse claims. And the church's members do, sometimes handling groups of venomous rattlers at once, bouncing uncontrollably, occasionally being bit, now and again dying from the poison. But in The Guardian's photo exhibit, there are also occasional shots of a guitar player. And it's the music, from this very church, that not only accompanies this endangered, radical Christian practice, but which is also the focus of Sublime Frequencies' West Virginia Snake Handler Revival, the first album the Seattle-based label has ever released featuring music recorded in the United States. Not surprisingly, Ian Brennan, known for recordings of music made by endangered communities all over the globe, produced this record. And despite these folks' feudal views on homosexuals and women, musically, this is likely some of the most over the top, hypnotic rock and roll transcendence to ever be captured on tape. "He is #1" is the ultimate proof. The track, led by the frantic, in-the-red vocals of Pastor Chris Wolford, features guitars and drums chugging out a monotonous one-chord vamp covered in swamp muck. They chew on that chord, cranking a possessed telecaster-infused, amplified stomp out into the hollers, driving with a stamina that would make Junior Kimbrough proud. Wolford, undoubtedly drenched in sweat, hollers, whoops, insinuates, and punctuates every phrase with "huh," as is typical for hardcore preachers all over the southern US. At 13 minutes, it's nearly too much to bear. There's a reason this is the album's final track. But there are plenty of other examples of this album's disturbing power. The opening track, the one minute "Spirit of God," features Wolford's voice, a capella, doused in echo, as if he's testifying deep within an abandoned mine shaft. "Jesus Has to be #1," is not unlike the LP's finale, though it's much shorter. Here, Wolford screams "Aah Gawd," and it's terrifying. Elsewhere, other people sing, with haunted, determined results. The vocalist on "I'm a Lord Jesus Man" is never on key, and the music is better for it. Here is the style of many a 1960s or 70s-era trucker anthem, complete with slithering guitar licks and grooves made for the highway. Later, Wolford returns, exhorting about forgetting to take his ADHD meds and instead getting jacked up on Starbucks. He screams, pants, and grunts, nearly obliterating the wall of electric thrum behind him. Some of the intensity found here is manipulated. The brief track, "Rock and Roll was stolen from God by Satan," for example, features anonymous testimony over a guitar and drum loop. "Maybe I Won't Do What I Said I'd Do" loops the title repeatedly over a duplicated demonic laugh for 22 seconds. But by and large, Brennan left the tapes alone, leaving the music's pugnaciousness be. Nothing here was created for commercial purposes. Instead, it documents a music that hasn't budged stylistically in 50 years, rampaging somewhere between hillbilly boogie, and rock and roll choogle. It's a natural, amplified soundtrack to small congregations of people whose practice has connections to other deep, unyielding trance ritual around the globe, from Gnawa in Morocco, to ecstatic nightclub DJs in Berlin, to the electrified molam that accompanies the Phi Ta Khon festival of ghosts in NE Thailand. Further reading: Peni Candra Rini - Wani Alhousseini Anivolla & Girum Mezmur - Afropentatonism Photo documentary in The Guardian Hear more of the album. items.body: Review by ProgfanJP — Formed in 2023 around guitarist Fernando de la Figuera, who cites King Crimson and Robert Fripp as his primary influences, the band came together when drummer Fran Gazol and bassist Mart�n Gros joined the fold. Their debut album arrives in 2025 through Spanish label Astronomy Recording Music, released on CD.The band's sound takes King Crimson's 1980s-2000s era as its foundation and channels it into math rock territory reminiscent of Polyphia and Animals as Leaders. Central to it all is de la Figuera's technically commanding guitar work, with high-speed arpeggios and cross-picking that carry the direct stamp of Robert Fripp, while a muscular bass and explosively dynamic drumming respond in kind. The balance between advanced technique and precisely composed, note-perfect arrangements is pulled off with a naturalness that's hard to fake.The rhythmic structures are complex throughout, but the album leans into four-beat grooves often enough that the bright, major-key melodies get room to breathe, pushing the overall feel closer to the punch of emo and melodic hardcore than to King Crimson's heavier, more aggressive side.Standout moments include "Radical", which the band themselves call their calling card, built on ostinato guitar figures reminiscent of "Fracture" and restless rhythmic shifts that generate a peculiar sense of weightlessness. "Planet 503" heads in a more symphonic direction, with synth pedal textures and lyrical melodies that lift the whole thing into proper progressive rock territory.More than just homage, this is an ambitious debut that announces a genuinely distinctive voice in the genre.
items._cn_summary: 这张2025年的西班牙前卫摇滚首作以King Crimson八十至两千年代风格为根基，融合了Polyphia与Animals as Leaders式的数学摇滚技巧。吉他手Fernando de la Figuera的高速分解和弦与交叉弹拨带有明显的Robert Fripp印记，搭配强劲的贝斯与爆发力十足的鼓点。复杂多变的节奏结构中穿插四拍律动，明亮的大调旋律让整体气质更接近情绪硬核与旋律硬核，而非King Crimson的沉重侵略面。专辑在致敬与个人表达之间取得一定平衡，技术层面精准且展现出独立音乐语言。由西班牙独立厂牌Astronomy Recording Music发行。

items.body: Blone Noble Dominator Mystic Transfers We had very little idea what to expect when Blone Noble took the stage at Verboden Festival here in Vancouver last weekend, but were won over almost instantly by the Los Angeles art pop act’s combination of theatrical whimsy, and easy to groove to songs. Recent EP Dominator cinches the one-man show’s charms via a fairly omnivorous combination of electronic pop sounds and pure, undiluted personality. Opener “High Society” gets to the point quickly in both the original and Kontravoid remixes, layering samples, octave bass, and crooned vocals, along with a kitchen sink’s worth of vocal and guitar samples, house pianos and acid lines that are somehow corralled together into a funky whole. “Body Fascination” goes more minimal, with a simple combination of synths and drums, the song’s appeal coming from the vocal switch ups, half falsetto, half processed into weird mutant shapes. The title track is presented in both its normal version and a remix from “Tony Price” and differs considerably in each form; the former is a dance punky joint with a laidback vibe, Lou Reed by way of the discotheque, where the remix transforms the song into a hot slice of balaeric techno, all sunny vibes and drum machine shake. It’s a fun, mildly puzzling, but undeniably enjoyable suite of songs that captures Blone Noble’s charms ably. Dominator by Blone Noble Child Of Night Conspiracy Phage Tapes If you happened to have checked out Ohio duo Child Of Night’s 2021 debut The Walls At Dawn, a number of surprises await on new LP Conspiracy, none of which are unpleasant. One is the presence of a record this melodic on a label as traditionally harsh as Phage Tapes, but most important is a decided shift away from a holistic approach to moody darkwave and towards a classic, chilly vein of synthpop. The icy chirp of opener “Old Moons”‘ perky but minimal synth leads is backed by a restrained bed of supporting programming recalling either the halcyon days of Mute releases or millennial bedroom synthpop, take your pick. While one or two cuts on Child Of Night’s debut played about with these sounds, they’re the sustained focus of Conspiracy, with everything from “Complacent”‘s impatient angst to the pensive pulse of closer “The Very Last Time” holding just a patina of analog haze and echo across all their elements. There’s something of a paucity of fully-developed and memorable songs in and of themselves on the record, with individual grooves, moments, and licks standing out more than full tracks after a few listens, but the catchy vocal refrain on “It’s Cold In Here”, or the psychedelic synth squalls on “Controlled Burn” which bring The Glove to mind, all have a charm suited to Child Of Night’s new direction. Conspiracy by C.O.N. The post Observer: Blone Noble & Child Of Night appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 本辑为两支美国艺人的作品合评。Blone Noble为洛杉矶单人艺术流行项目，EP《Dominator》将电子流行、浩室钢琴、酸屋音色、巴尔亚利卡铁克诺等元素杂糅，以戏剧化舞台感和多样化人声处理为标识。Child Of Night来自俄亥俄，LP《Conspiracy》在以硬核噪音闻名的Phage Tapes厂牌发行，风格从暗潮氛围转向偏经典路线的冷调合成器流行，参考Mute厂牌千禧年时期的卧室电子风格。两张作品在旋律性与可听性上较为突出，Blone Noble侧重舞曲声响的拼贴与个性化表达，Child Of Night强调模拟合成器质感和忧郁氛围；整体风格更接近独立电子与合成器流行的主流面向，跨界融合与实验性元素相对有限。

items._cn_summary: 这是一张收录1930至1950年代希腊乡村民间音乐（demotika）的档案合辑，音乐风格根植于拜占庭时期的传统，主题涵盖爱情、死亡、婚姻与自然。曲目以Syrtos风格的挽歌式吟唱和Pidiktos节奏的欢快民间舞蹈为主，保留了纯粹的传统演奏与演唱方式。合辑来自独立小厂牌DINTE，具有明确的地域文化价值，展现了希腊本土及散居社区的音乐传统。由于该作品为纯传统民谣档案，缺乏与实验、电子或当代爵士等元素的融合，与用户偏好的实验前卫及跨界方向距离较远，但其世界音乐属性和文化独特性仍具有一定的聆听价值。

items._cn_summary: Beatrice M.的首张全长专辑《Sinking》由英国地下低音厂牌Tectonic发行，是一张以dubstep为核心的电子乐作品。艺术家具有法英双重文化背景，此前通过Bait、Tempa、SPE:C等独立厂牌发行的12寸单曲积累了声誉。整张专辑近一小时，在dubstep的框架内探索"粗糙与平滑"的平衡，融合微妙的感性氛围与强劲的律动推进力，节奏模式涵盖rolling、stepping、skanking等多种变体。作品在传统dubstep与其衍生形态之间游走，体现出一定的实验倾向。整体定位为地下电子乐场景中的低音音乐制作，风格偏向bass music而非IDM或ambient方向。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国电子音乐人Arovane与美国声音艺术家Taylor Deupree合作推出，是两人继2022年12k厂牌合作之后的第二次联手。作品以循环音段和多层次处理为核心手法，通过反复处理和再加工的声音构建出一条具有有机感的听觉旅程，呈现出氛围电子与微观声音领域的典型美学。两位艺术家各自在IDM、ambient和实验电子领域有着深厚积累，合作将即兴触感与精密的声音设计相结合。LAAPS作为独立小众厂牌保证了作品的地下实验属性。整体定位偏向抽象声响探索，适合偏好电子实验与氛围音乐的听众，但由于评论内容较为简短且接近新闻稿性质，无法深入评估其具体的艺术突破与创新程度。

items.body: Gabriele Poso has been releasing music since 2008, through Yoruba Records, BBE, Soundway, Wonderwheel and Mr. Bongo. For his sixth album he started his own imprint, AG Records, and recorded Maraviglia live to tape with a full band in an analogue studio in southern Italy. “Contigo Mi Vida” is the second single from the album, out on 19 June. Emanuele Coluccia leads on horns, moving between saxophone, flute and trumpet over Afro-Cuban percussion and a groove rooted in late-’70s Italian disco and Afrobeat. Poso’s vocals run effected and dubbed-out through it. Maraviglia also features Andrea Rossetti on piano, Fender Rhodes, Hammond and Moog, Davide Codazzo on bass, Antonio De Donno on drums and percussion and Alberto Zacà on guitar. Listen to “Contigo Mi Vida” HERE and pre-order Maraviglia via THIS LINK The post Daily. Discovery: Gabriele Poso – Contigo Mi Vida appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 意大利音乐人Gabriele Poso第六张专辑《Maraviglia》的第二支单曲，融合了Afro-Cuban打击乐、七十年代意大利迪斯科律动与Afrobeat元素，在意大利南部模拟录音室以全乐队同期录音方式完成。人声经过效果器处理呈现dub化质感，编曲中管乐（萨克斯、长笛、小号）在打击乐与贝斯线上自由穿梭，键盘部分涵盖钢琴、Fender Rhodes、Hammond与Moog。整体定位偏向世界音乐与放克律动的跨文化融合，模拟录音与dub处理为作品增添了一定的实验色彩，但核心仍属律动导向的舞曲化制作。原文为单曲宣传新闻稿，篇幅较短，缺乏深度评论内容。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Excesses...in arrangements, in length, nothing was enough for the successor to Don Giovanni, and Le Tr'sor de Valliesres, Versailles' third album, boasts the colors of many macarons mimicking a rainbow. Guillaume de la Piliere sings and plays guitar as if it were the most furious rock, but with Alain de Lille on piano and keyboards, creating that palatial symphonic atmosphere...which, being French, always has a guillotine lurking about...half threat, half hope, depending on your perspective. The cabaret piano perfectly complements the streetwise edge, giving freshness to the complex arrangements and making them immediate, coexisting with Renaissance-like sections where the band becomes precise and brings together the land of Charles Aznavour and Johnny Hallyday with Rush and Genesis.Exquise Betise continues to create grandiose atmospheres like Genesis, but with a prominence in the execution of the drums, bass, and keyboards that leaves no time to trace influences... instead, it immerses you in the offered proposition, full of subtleties and pure symphonic rock with a French touch. Une Saint Barthelemy Devote has that folkloric tenor present in Foxtrot, along with the musicality of Michel Berger, and bass lines by Olivier de Gency without which it wouldn't be the same. Alain de Lille's keyboards are reminiscent of the early, raw Tony Banks of Nursery Cryme.And the next section becomes both rock and psychedelic, with synthesizers and a chorus in which everyone participates. They speed up...and stop speeding up...only to do it again, discovering new sounds in the process. In the middle there are parts that recall Pink Floyd's Echoes, but then their virtuoso execution takes them to other territories, the guitar here with a David Gilmour sound at the service of the infidelities in carved walls, secret passageways, and organs that hide surprises like Magma-style choirs, while a jazzy piano improvises...breaking schemes, challenging the monarchy with the sharpest anarchy.In Viendra L'heure the electric guitar together with the keyboard carve an ornate canvas on which they will sing, with Guillaume as soloist, reaching the enveloping psychedelia of The Doors, until a wind unites the theme to the next, the flamenco Jadis, where the spirit of Steve Hackett floats alongside Manuel de Falla.Degenerescence Obsessionnelle takes over with counterpoints of bass and guitar...bathed by the keyboard like the sea bathes the beach, and yes...Hackett is heard again, along with a harpsichord, until a keyboard section like a choir with bass and mellotron that recalls Yes, recreates the atmosphere of Heart of the Sunrise, only until Guillaume sings and the melody, half longing for the past, half promise of the future, continues on. At times Olivier de Gency sounds like Chris Squire without sounding like an imitation, and there are moments where they take flight and sound like themselves, a product of the place that saw them born and gave them their imprint; there we see the Galeries Lafayette, as well as the Banlieues de La Goutte d'Or.That street-style Hammond organ rock from the beginning returns in Avec Tous Mes Hommages, full of harmony in the keyboard and guitar notes...playing classic hard rock solos, until the whole band sounds like the best Yes in blue, blanc et rouge.Le Tresor des Valliesres ends as the album began, with an explosion of colors suggested by the keyboard and guitar notes, a cathedral under whose wide roof whispers burrow, as well as stretched notes...until dissonant guitar and bass notes, as if King Crimson were forcibly taking the farewell, and the atonality throws off balance...paradoxically, to increase the level reached, it confirms with each note that freedom, which makes us live in equality, and only in this way will fraternity arrive.
items._cn_summary: 法国交响前卫摇滚乐队Versailles的第三张专辑，将华丽繁复的管弦化编曲与法式卡巴莱钢琴、弗拉门戈、法国香颂等元素相结合，呈现出浓郁的法国文化色彩。作品中可辨识出Genesis、Yes、Pink Floyd、Rush等经典前卫摇滚的影响痕迹，并融入Magma式的合唱段落与文艺复兴风格的对位段落。整体定位偏向传统交响前卫范畴，以宏大叙事和复杂编曲见长，但在实验性与avant-garde层面的探索较为有限，更多是在经典谱系内的精致化演绎。吉他手兼主唱的演绎充满摇滚张力，键盘手对Tony Banks早期风格的致敬清晰可辨，贝斯线条也带有Chris Squire式的特点。对于偏好传统交响前卫的听众具有一定吸引力，但对追求更激进声响实验的听众而言，其创新力度略显保守。

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — I'll say it right away to avoid misunderstandings: Prog is back!! And it comes once again from the North.The album is part of Jordsj�'s tenth anniversary celebrations. Initially conceived as a collection of unreleased tracks recorded in the studio between 2020 and 2025, the project then took on a life of its own, with the pieces intertwining thematically exploring themes such as war, chaos, the fall of rulers and the dawn of a new period, as well as cults and sects.The album was created, arranged and mixed entirely by the two founding members:H�kon Oftung (Multi-instrumentalist: guitars, flute, keyboards, vocals), leader of the group and leading figure in the psychedelic and progressive underground scene in Oslo. He has collaborated over time with cult bands such as Tusm�rke, The Chronicles of Father Robin, Wobbler and Zenon, just to name a few.Kristian Fr�land (Drums, percussion, production), childhood friend of Oftung and long-time partner in the Jordsj� project. In addition to taking care of the acoustic rhythm section, he personally took care of the production and mixing of Pestkr�nikene, giving the album its peculiar 70s analog sound.Prominent artists have been invited to contribute significantly to specific tracks.Jon A. Henriksen, multi-instrumentalist and singer, lends his voice to the songs "White Magic" and "Talisman II". He is the creator of Black Magic, a Norwegian band that started as a heavy/doom/black metal project and then veered towards 70s hard rock sounds. He collaborated with H�kon Oftung for many years in Black Magic.Kristian Valbo, well-known extreme metal drummer of the historic Norwegian bands Obliteration and Aura Noir, takes care of the drums, rototoms and artwork of the song "Spiritual Lament". For this album he demonstrated his crossover versatility by playing percussion and doing the cover art.Lars Fredrik Fr�islie, keyboardist and mastermind of Wobbler, one of the leading bands of modern symphonic prog, performs a MiniMoog synthesizer solo on the track "Kaosveldets Endelikt". He is a great fan and collector of vintage keyboards (Mellotron, Hammond, Moog), with which he recreates atmospheres faithful to the early 70s.Andreas Prestmo, lead singer and lyricist of The Wobbler, as well as frontman of The Chronicles of Father Robin, is the guest vocalist on the song "The Awakened". He is famous in the Scandinavian scene for his evocative and theatrical vocal lines, ideal for the mythological lyrics of Jordsj�.The title "Pestkr�nikene" means "The Plague Chronicles" in Norwegian. This title embodies the central idea of the album: a dark and mythological concept album that revolves around destruction, distorted faith and the rebirth that follows. The songs on the album are connected by a coherent theme and lyrics, based on four fundamental elements: war and destruction, the collapse of old social structures; the fall of kings, the brutal end of kingdoms, monarchs and empires; sects and cults, religious and spiritual fanaticism in times of crisis; It is the dawn of a new era, the birth of a new period from the ruins of devastation.In this apocalyptic context, the band blends its hard rock and heavy metal roots with folk and psychedelic elements, creating a real "sound alchemy" to tell the eternal cycle of death and rebirth.The album alternates sung songs with entirely instrumental compositions, in perfect Scandinavian progressive rock style. The vocal tracks are "Pestkr�nikene" (in Norwegian), "White Magic", "Seven Heads", "The Awakened", "Spiritual Lament" and "Talisman II" (all in English). Instead, "Kaosvelde" and "Kaosveldets Endelikt" are completely instrumental.I particularly appreciate the use of the Norwegian language in their songs since always, which makes them archaic, solemn, mystical and profound. On this album, the English-language songs are no different, they manage to evoke the same feeling thanks to the splendid interpretations.This album was made with an artisanal and vintage approach, far from modern and digital productions. The sound is rich and warm, created with iconic analog keyboards such as the MiniMoog and the Mellotron that weaves orchestral sound carpets. The Hammond organ and piano, then, drive the main melodies with timeless class. The hard rock energy is perfectly balanced by dreamy and acoustic sections, creating an immersive and dynamic atmosphere.The flute, played by H�kon Oftung, remains one of the band's hallmarks, intertwining with guitars and recalling the greats of progressive rock. Despite the complex structures and the continuous changes of tempo, the structured suites and the symphonic atmospheres typical of northern European prog (inspired by Scandinavian bands such as Landberk, �nglag�rd and the Wobbler themselves), the album is compact, with a total duration of only 36 minutes, a real concentrate of energy and creativity."Pestkr�nikene", a song sung in Norwegian, opens the album with an immediate immersion in the band's new 70s hard rock sound. Powerful guitar riffs alternate with soothing flute sections, creating an atmosphere that oscillates between tension and relaxation. The song explores the theme of cyclical time, with the "plague" representing the social and moral collapse that is repeated every time humanity forgets history and breaks the balance. H�kon Oftung deftly juggles sharp guitars and a dreamlike flute, while Kristian Fr�land's rhythm section adds a touch of vintage analogue warmth. The main riff, inspired by classic hard/prog, is simply splendid."White Magic", a song sung in English, is one of the catchiest songs on the album, its hypnotic and decidedly psychedelic rhythm, combined with folk influences, creates an atmospheric rock that immediately enters the head while maintaining a complex structure. The song describes the dynamics of psychological manipulation within cults, with the "White Magic Man" seducing the minds of his fifty followers with utopian promises that work like a drug ("poppy seeds"). Jon A. Henriksen, with his theatrical and charismatic voice, perfectly interprets the ambiguity of the cult leader. The song has an extremely engaging chorus. The countermelodies are beautiful and the mood is both positive and expresses an atmosphere of urgency. When the song slows down there is a great guitar solo with exceptional sustain. Great song."Seven Heads", a song sung in English, enhances the darker and heavier side of the band, touching primitive doom rock but resulting in sudden symphonic melodic moments dominated by the Mellotron. The apocalyptic symbolism is evident: the "Seven Heads" refer to the biblical Beast and symbolize the destructive arrogance of declining political and religious power. Oftung's work on vintage keyboards (Hammond organ and Mellotron) creates a majestic wall of sound that emphasizes the sense of impending catastrophe. The backbone groove of the excellent rhythm section is composed of multiple inlays and chisellings. The alternation of flute and guitar when the atmosphere becomes tense is splendid. The central tempo change, which transports the piece into a spooky atmosphere is absolutely great. Great vocal interpretation at the end of the song, when he returns to the hard rhythm, of an extraordinary rock. Textbook closure. Beautiful piece."Kaosvelde - Vasallens Elegi" is the first fully instrumental track on the album, a jewel of progressive folk, with acoustic guitars and flute that intertwine in an elegant way, evoking a woody and melancholic atmosphere reminiscent of the Scandinavian tradition of the early 70s. It is the lament of a vassal who helplessly witnesses the chaos that invades his kingdom, marking the end of the old feudal order. Oftung's acoustic performance is impeccable, and Fr�land's minimal and evocative percussion marks an almost solemn tempo, in a slow and continuous credendo that briefly seems to accelerate but then returns imposing and solemn. The central flute solo is poignant and dreamlike, and adds a touch of melancholy to the narrative."Kaosveldets Endelikt", a completely instrumental track, is the sequel to the previous track to which it is inextricably fused, but this time in an electric and majestic key. The style shifts towards a more complex symphonic prog and a fast tempo with Heavy Metal accents, describing the final act of the collapse of the kings. Primordial chaos takes over, wiping out corrupt hierarchies. Lars Fredrik Fr�islie's intervention is extraordinary, with a virtuoso MiniMoog analog synthesizer solo cutting through the track like lightning, an exceptional solo explosion. Great energy and transport not without clich�s typical of the genre and of fine workmanship. The guitars are often doubled and the drums are metronomic with thrilling rolls. Great piece,"The Awakened", a song sung in English, is a theatrical, dynamic and dramatic song. The sound combines structural complexity with airy and solemn vocal melodies typical of Nordic symphonic rock. The focus shifts to the survivors, forced to walk through the rubble with a new, painful spiritual self-awareness after the catastrophe. The guest voice of Andreas Prestmo is the fulcrum of the piece; its timbre gives an epic and poignant tone to the narrative. The mood and voice are very prog, the excellent guitar riff alternates in a game of back and forth with the keyboards. The intertwining of Prestmo's vocal lines and Mellotron's carpets is splendid, creating an evocative and engaging atmosphere. Monstrous bass throughout the song, sharp guitar."Spiritual Lament", a song sung in English, is a deep and reflective track, with a ritual atmosphere. The tones become more intense and decidedly rock, abandoning the lightness of folk to embrace a psychedelic sound full of emotions. The beginning is very King Crimson. It represents an inner journey of grieving and searching for peace, symbolizing the spiritual emptiness that a person can feel when his old material certainties are lost. Kristian Valbo on drums introduces the rototoms, giving a powerful and tribal rhythm. The song is animated by an amazing bass line with which the guitar dialogues wonderfully. Rich and powerful battery. The splendid voice of a beautiful vocal enters about halfway through the song after a long instrumental section and the song becomes more folk, before resuming the initial mood that with the voice becomes epic and imposing. Towards the end the atmosphere becomes decidedly psychedelic and is the basis for a stratospheric guitar solo. The closing was beautiful. Great drums that stand out in this beautiful piece."Talisman II", a song sung in English, is the perfect conclusion to the album. An epic track that mixes hard rock with the tempo changes typical of symphonic prog, culminating in an emotional finale that leaves a sense of completeness. The talisman, a magical and symbolic object guardian of knowledge, is essential to overcome difficult times and start a new era of rebirth. Jon A. Henriksen returns to vocals to support Oftung, closing the conceptual circle of the album. The final interaction between electric guitar, synthesizers and drums is magnificent, and the final instrumental coda is liberating and beautifully arranged. There is a folk mood that never disappears. The entries overlap and complement each other. A song of extraordinary structure and power, powerful even in the most folk phase, it explodes in the epic phases. The singing and the piece as a whole are extraordinary.Pestkr�nikene is an album that is like a journey through time through a mix of musical genres performed with great skill and blended together in a brilliant way, a sound experience that blends hard rock and classic heavy metal of the 70s with typical atmospheres of progressive rock, folk and psychedelic, without losing contact with the Scandinavian tradition. Compared to Jordsj�'s previous pastoral and acoustic works, this album stands out for a more powerful and decisive sound, a real tribute to the heaviest hard rock scene of those years. The voices and performances of the individual musicians are splendid, a screaming rhythm section.Essential album, so far the best of 2026. Prog is back!!
items._cn_summary: Jordsjø的《Pestkrønikene》是一张挪威交响前卫摇滚概念专辑，以瘟疫、战争、帝国崩塌与邪教崇拜为核心主题，呈现出黑暗神话式的叙事框架。专辑由两位创始成员全权创作、编曲与混音，特别强调70年代模拟音色质感，邀请了多位挪威地下音乐人参与客串，其中包括极端金属鼓手与Wobbler键盘手等。音乐风格根植于复古交响前卫传统，在器乐编排上较为扎实，跨界引入了一些硬摇滚和金属元素，但整体仍以70年代致敬为核心取向。黑暗的概念主题与部分氛围营造能触及暗潮/哥特审美，但声音设计偏保守，实验性与创新性有限。

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — Not counting the various archival releases I've covered before, Malibran's sophomore album, Le Porte Del Silenzio, will be the first review I publish of an album recorded and released in the nineties. When it comes to Rock Progressivo Italiano overall, I haven't quite touched this era of the genre as I should have. Beyond these guys I really only know Nuova Era and D.F.A., so I still have some exploring to do here. Moving on, I would say this is a really strong retro Italian prog record, utilizing predominantly instrumental passages to exercise a very powerful and melodic style of progressive rock. One thing I wish was changed were some of the English lyrics, which sort of breaks the overall flow, as Italian ones would've fit the music better. Beyond that, this album is still very consistent and full of interesting symphonic prog with tons of neat little details and material to dig your teeth into, all within the grips of a very captivating album cover that seems to recall greatly to the work of Roger Dean with his art for Yes, specifically the cover of Relayer. The music here is very strong, fusing both keyboard and rhythm-driven progressive rock with thoroughly put-together neo-prog. It stays steady musically, not really losing my interest and always making for a fun experience. At some points it feels like the band can meander in this format for a while and just blend everything in together, which can feel a little too straightforward, but overall, there is some really nice material on here. The majority of the songs are ten minutes or under, with my favorites of these being the opening Livin' Alone and the driving Libero, which each seem to have more energy put into them and have the most satisfying moments in terms of technicality. That would be the case if it weren't for the monstrous ending to the album, the twenty-seven-minute-long title track, which is easily my favorite piece on the record. It's very emotionally charged but not sacrificing pure energy and chaos, where on most of the songs it seems to be fused together, this one keeps the sections more separate, distinct, and memorable. In conclusion, I would say this is a very fine example of retro Rock Progressivo Italiano and does a nice take on the classic sound while still sounding modern. Maybe not an essential as a whole, but seriously underrated in terms of exposure and definitely worth checking out if you want to get into more recent Italian prog. I'll be rewarding this one a strong 4/5.
items._cn_summary: Malibran乐队1993年发行的第二张专辑《Le Porte Del Silenzio》属于意大利复古前卫摇滚范畴，融合交响前卫与新前卫元素。作品以器乐段落为主，键盘与节奏驱动的编曲构成核心，大量细节值得反复聆听。二十七分钟长的同名终曲是专辑最突出的篇章，情绪饱满且结构清晰，各段落独立而完整。整体而言，这是一张忠实承袭七十年代意大利前卫摇滚传统的作品，在经典声响基础上保持现代感，但在实验性与创新性上较为保守，更偏向传统流派的稳健延续。封面设计借鉴了Roger Dean的风格。

items.body: Norwegian darkwave and cyberpunk duo Rule of Two have released a cover of Depeche Mode’s “It’s No Good“. The Rule of Two “It’s No Good” version is accompanied by an official music video directed by band member Kristian Liljan. The cover is Rule of Two’s fifth single of 2026, following “Afterlife” via Polypiel Records on May 7 and “All Time Low” in February. ‘It’s No Good’: the original “It’s No Good” was released on March 31, 1997, as the second single from Depeche Mode’s ninth studio album “Ultra” (Mute Records, April 14, 1997). The track was written by Martin Gore and produced by Tim Simenon, recorded at Eastcote Studios in London and Larrabee West in Los Angeles, and mixed at Abbey Road Studios. It reached number five in the United Kingdom and number one in Denmark, Spain, Sweden and on the US Billboard Dance Club Play chart. About Rule of Two Rule of Two is a darkwave and cyberpunk duo formed in Oslo, Norway, in 2023 by Ronny Flissundet and Kristian Liljan, both from the Oslo metal and alternative rock underground with prior activity in Damokles, Dunderbeist and Kite. The project blends eerie synthesizers, mechanical rhythms and glitch textures into a sound the duo describes as taking a darker, more industrial direction with each release. Their debut album “Aiming for the Sun” was announced by Side-Line in November 2025. The “It’s No Good” cover, out June 4, 2026, is their first cover of a Depeche Mode track.
items._cn_summary: 挪威双人组Rule of Two以暗潮与赛博朋克为基底，融合阴森的合成器音色、机械化节奏与故障质感，整体方向趋向更黑暗与工业化的声音探索。该作品为对Depeche Mode经典曲目《It's No Good》的翻唱，所属厂牌为独立厂牌Polypiel Records。乐队成员均来自奥斯陆金属与另类摇滚地下场景，融合了EBM、后朋克与暗潮元素。原文为新闻稿性质的文章，侧重于发布信息与背景介绍，缺乏对翻唱版本具体音乐处理、编曲差异及艺术价值的深入评析。作为翻唱作品，其原创性受到一定限制，但乐队在工业电子与暗潮交叉领域的探索方向仍值得关注。
